← Oxford game library

Geography: build, investigate, revise

116 activities covering 58 topics, with two practical missions in each activity. There are 29 activities in each player mode. The collection uses 18 shared interaction families, matched to the topic; these are not 116 separate simulation engines.

Run a lesson

  1. Choose Geography, grade and player mode. Open an activity and review its practice source.
  2. Edit the mission brief and expand the mission settings to change locations, cards, measurements, clues, constraints or model values. Update the brief when changing its data. Save to My lessons or download a lesson file for another device.
  3. Teams choose 2–6 names. Each team locks its response before the shared review. Two-player activities use independent simultaneous touch panels; neither panel is secret.
  4. Open Mission brief & evidence, then construct a solution. Tap controls also work with keyboard. Maps and sorting cards support drag-and-drop; routes, charts and landscapes support touch tracing.
  5. Test my work checks the constructed result. An unsuccessful test gives feedback and leaves the work editable. A successful mission starts at 100 points, with 10 points deducted per unsuccessful test, to a minimum of 20. Reset and undo do not erase those attempts. Finish & review submits an unfinished mission for zero points.
  6. Discuss why the solution works. The automatic check assesses the configured model, not the quality of a student’s spoken explanation. Rotate the student at the board for whole-class activities.

Different ways to show understanding

  • Build a map
  • Navigate a route
  • Connect a network
  • Reconstruct a timeline
  • Sort a field collection
  • Repair a report
  • Build an explanation
  • Pack and test a plan
  • Negotiate resources
  • Run a glacier laboratory
  • Run a river laboratory
  • Draw a landscape profile
  • Plot field data
  • Investigate a mystery
  • Plan with map layers
  • Collect a field sample
  • Draw a scaled blueprint
  • Sculpt a landscape

Examples include drawing a scaled plan, tracing a viable route, connecting a branching water cycle, allocating scarce water, controlling a glacier over several years, changing river energy to sort sediment, plotting measurements, building a terrain cross-section, collecting a stratified sample and removing unsupported claims from a report.

Practice sources and adaptations

The original attachment supplied ideas rather than the textbook pages, photographs, case-study datasets or climate graphs. Activities use authored practice sources and clearly labelled fictional datasets where those materials were unavailable. Replace these with your assigned evidence before assessing textbook-specific recall. Schematic grids are not navigation maps; their stated coordinates and scales belong to the exercise. Token budgets, glacier mass and sediment energy are simplified classroom models.

Physical construction, hidden partner materials, interviews and long written responses have been adapted for a public shared smartboard. Some interaction families recur across topics where they fit. The original idea and both implemented missions are shown below so teachers can judge the adaptation.

Earlier saved Geography lessons using the original question-based controls remain supported. Open a current library activity to use the new missions.

SoloNavigate a route

Low-impact safari: Fictional reserve grid: shaded habitat is off limits. Reach the viewing point via the guide station without entering protected ground. Trace adjacent squares; retrace one square to undo.

Plan with map layers

Planning desk for 7.9 Safari tourism. This fictional local grid tests how overlapping layers change a decision. Toggle each layer, compare constraints, then place one approved site. Inspect all three layers. Choose a site with service access (2), outside hazard (1) and protected land (3).

87.9 Safari tourismGuide and Conservationist
Original ideaNegotiate a tourism activity using different evidence, then acknowledge a remaining limitation.
2 PlayerNegotiate resources

Negotiate a fictional 10-token resource plan. Each stakeholder has a minimum agreement and a maximum useful allocation. Meet all agreements without overspending, then explain who received any extra resources. Several allocations are valid.

Pack and test a plan

Pack a practical plan within both the token and equipment-weight limits. Cover every mission need. Combined projects cover both named needs. More than one feasible plan may work. Costs and weights are classroom planning tokens, not real quotations.

87.10 Kenya’s developmentKenya: The Whole-Class Verdict
Original ideaEveryone contributes an indicator, example, or limitation to answer “How is Kenya doing?” collectively.
Whole ClassRepair a report

An editor has mixed accurate findings with unsupported claims. Cross out every unsupported sentence and preserve the defensible findings. Use the source, not how confident a sentence sounds.

Build an explanation

Build an evidence-based explanation. Put the conclusion in Claim, observations in Evidence, and the connection or caution in Reasoning. Read the finished argument aloud and defend it.
